checklist.step: Refresh the ICT audit universe against the DORA framework
actions: Break the ICT risk management framework into auditable units mirroring DORA Arts. 5-16 - governance and organisation, ICT risk identification, protection and prevention, detection, response and recovery, backup and restoration, learning and evolving, communication, plus Art. 24-25 testing and Arts. 28-30 third-party risk.
Add each auditable unit to the AuditBoard universe with an owner, the supporting CIF systems and the last audit date.
Reconcile the universe to the ICT risk register in the GRC platform so no top ICT risk lacks an auditable unit.
Have the Chief Info Security Officer and the Chief Risk Officer confirm the universe is complete and record their confirmation.
checklist.done: the ICT audit universe covers every DORA framework domain, reconciles to the ICT risk register and is confirmed by the CISO and CRO.

checklist.step: Score each auditable unit and build the risk-based plan
actions: Score each unit on inherent ICT risk, control maturity from the last audit, time since last coverage, incident history from the incident register, and CIF dependency.
Set frequency from the score - high-risk units annually, medium every two years, low every three - and record the rule applied on each unit.
Draft the plan with engagement names, quarters, budgeted days and the lead auditor for each.
Show explicitly which units are not covered next year and why, so the audit committee approves the gaps knowingly.
checklist.done: every auditable unit has a documented risk score, a derived frequency and either a scheduled engagement or a stated, approved coverage gap.

checklist.step: Evidence the ICT competence of the auditors assigned
actions: For each ICT engagement list the assigned auditors and record their ICT qualifications - CISA, CISSP, CRISC, cloud certifications - and their relevant prior engagement history.
Where in-house competence does not cover a domain such as cloud architecture or threat-led penetration testing, engage a co-source specialist and record the scope they cover.
Confirm no assigned auditor previously designed, implemented or operated the control they will audit, and record the independence check.
Store the competence and independence evidence against the engagement record before fieldwork starts, as Art. 6(6) requires auditors with sufficient ICT knowledge, skills and expertise.
checklist.done: every ICT engagement has documented auditor competence, any co-source scope, and a recorded independence check filed before fieldwork.

checklist.step: Get the audit committee to approve the plan before year end
actions: Table the plan with the risk scores, the coverage gaps, the resource requirement and the co-source budget.
State the DORA basis on the paper - Art. 6(6) requires the ICT risk management framework to be audited on a risk-based audit plan by auditors with sufficient ICT expertise.
Record the committee's approval, the version approved and any change it directs, and minute the challenge given to the coverage gaps.
Load the approved plan into AuditBoard as the baseline and lock it so in-year changes are visible as variances.
checklist.done: the audit committee has approved a named plan version before 31 December and the baseline is locked in AuditBoard.

checklist.step: Scope each ICT engagement against the framework requirements
actions: Write the engagement scope listing the DORA articles in scope, the controls to be tested from the GRC control library and the CIF systems the sample will be drawn from.
Agree the scope with the auditee - typically the Chief Info Security Officer or the Head of IT - and record any scope area they contest.
Set the test approach per control - inquiry plus inspection plus re-performance for key controls, with inquiry alone never sufficient for a key ICT control.
Issue the engagement letter with fieldwork dates, evidence request list and the report issue date.
checklist.done: each engagement has an agreed, article-referenced scope with a test approach per control and an issued engagement letter.

checklist.step: Execute fieldwork with evidence-based testing
actions: Pull system-generated evidence directly - IAM entitlement extracts, change records, scan results, backup restoration logs - rather than accepting management-prepared summaries.
For each key control select a sample with a documented method and record the seed, population and selection date in the workpaper.
Re-perform the control on the sample and record the result item by item, including the evidence reference for every exception.
Hold weekly clearance meetings with the auditee so factual disputes are settled during fieldwork, not after the report.
Have the engagement lead review and sign every workpaper before conclusions are drawn.
checklist.done: every key control has re-performed, system-sourced evidence on a documented sample, with reviewed and signed workpapers.

checklist.step: Grade findings and agree management actions with owners and dates
actions: Grade each finding critical, high, medium or low using the impact on a critical or important function and the likelihood of exploitation, not the ease of fixing it.
Write each finding with condition, criteria (the DORA article or internal standard), cause, effect and recommendation.
Obtain a written management response naming the action, the accountable owner at director level or above, and a specific date - responses of 'noted' or 'under review' are rejected.
Where management disputes a finding, record the disagreement and escalate unresolved critical items to the audit committee rather than softening the grade.
checklist.done: each finding carries a grade, a cited criterion, and a management response naming an action, a director-level owner and a date.

checklist.step: Issue the report to the audit committee and the management body
actions: Issue the final report with an overall opinion on the audited framework domain and the finding schedule with grades and dates.
Send it to the audit committee, the management body, the Chief Info Security Officer and the Chief Risk Officer, and record the distribution.
Present critical findings in person at the next audit committee meeting with the responsible executive present to answer.
Record the committee's directions and add any it gives as additional actions on the findings.
checklist.done: the report is issued with an opinion, distributed on the record and critical findings are presented in person with committee directions captured.

checklist.step: Run the formal follow-up process Art. 6(7) requires
actions: Load every finding into the follow-up register with owner, agreed date, grade and the verification method required at closure.
Send automated reminders to owners at T-30 and T-7 days and escalate to the owner's executive at T+1 day past due.
Require the owner to submit evidence of completion - not a status update - and refuse closure requests with no artefact attached.
Report the follow-up register to the audit committee every quarter, showing open critical findings by age band.
checklist.done: every finding sits in the follow-up register with reminders armed, and quarterly ageing of open critical findings reaches the audit committee.

checklist.step: Verify critical finding closure by re-performance, not assertion
actions: For each critical finding proposed for closure, re-run the original test on a fresh sample drawn after the remediation date.
Confirm the remediation addressed the cause recorded in the finding, not only the symptom the sample surfaced.
Where the re-test fails, reopen the finding with a new agreed date and report the failed closure to the audit committee.
Attach the re-performance workpaper to the finding before moving it to Closed-Verified.
checklist.done: no critical finding reaches Closed-Verified without a post-remediation re-performance workpaper attached.

checklist.step: Escalate overdue and disputed critical findings
actions: List every critical ICT finding more than 30 days past its agreed date with its owner and the reason given.
Require the accountable executive to attend the audit committee and either commit to a new date or request a formal risk acceptance.
For a risk acceptance, require a written statement of the residual exposure to critical or important functions and the compensating controls, signed by the Chief Risk Officer.
Minute the outcome and reflect accepted risks in the ICT risk register in the GRC platform.
checklist.done: every critical finding past 30 days has a committee-recorded outcome - a new date or a CRO-signed risk acceptance reflected in the risk register.

checklist.step: Track plan execution against the approved baseline
actions: Report quarterly on engagements completed, in progress, deferred and cancelled against the locked baseline.
Require audit committee approval for any deferral or cancellation of an ICT engagement, with the risk of not covering it stated.
Reallocate released days to the next highest-scoring uncovered unit rather than absorbing them.
Publish year-to-date plan completion percentage on the audit committee dashboard.
checklist.done: plan variances are reported quarterly and every ICT engagement deferral or cancellation carries a recorded committee approval.

checklist.step: Feed audit results back into the ICT risk framework
actions: Map each audit finding to the ICT risk register entry and control it affects and re-assess control effectiveness with the control owner.
Where audit disproved a control's design, mark the control ineffective in the GRC library until re-tested rather than waiting for remediation.
Update the Art. 6(5) framework document review record with what the audit changed.
Report the revised control effectiveness picture in the quarterly ICT risk report.
checklist.done: every finding is reflected in a re-assessed control and risk register entry, with disproved controls marked ineffective immediately.

checklist.step: Assess the audit function's own ICT capability annually
actions: Compare the ICT skills the plan requires - cloud, identity, resilience testing, third-party assurance - against the team's current certifications and experience.
Book the training needed in the learning management system and track completion by auditor.
Where a gap will persist through the year, secure co-source capacity before the engagement is scheduled rather than after it slips.
Report the capability assessment and the residual gaps to the audit committee with the plan.
checklist.done: an annual ICT capability assessment names the gaps, the booked training and the co-source cover, and is reported with the plan.

checklist.step: File the audit evidence pack for supervisory production
actions: Assemble the pack - audit universe, approved plan and committee minute, competence records, issued reports, management responses, follow-up register and closure verification workpapers.
File under DORA/Art-6-6/<year> with the 7-year retention label from report issue.
Index by DORA article, auditable unit, finding grade and status so a supervisor's question about one domain can be answered directly.
Record the pack location on the DORA obligation record for the 10 business day production service level.
checklist.done: the audit evidence pack is filed, retention-labelled and indexed by DORA article, auditable unit and finding status.

testing.step: Build the population of planned engagements, findings and auditors
actions: Export the locked approved ICT audit plan baseline with engagement names, quarters and lead auditors.
Export all ICT audit findings open at any point in the year with grade, raise date, agreed date, status and closure date.
Export the auditor roster actually charged to each ICT engagement from the time recording data rather than the plan.
Reconcile the three extracts and sign the population as complete with extract timestamps.
testing.done: plan, finding and auditor populations are extracted, reconciled and signed as complete with dated extracts.

testing.step: Reconcile executed engagements to the approved baseline
actions: Match each baseline engagement to an issued report and list every engagement with no report as a coverage gap.
For each gap check whether the audit committee minutes record an approved deferral or cancellation with the risk stated.
List any ICT engagement executed that was not in the approved baseline and check it was approved as an in-year addition.
Compute plan completion percentage independently of the dashboard figure.
testing.done: every baseline engagement is matched to a report or to a minuted committee approval, and completion percentage is recomputed.

testing.step: Draw a documented sample of engagements and findings
actions: Take 100 percent of critical findings and 100 percent of engagements covering a CIF-supporting domain.
Take 20 further findings at random from the remainder using a recorded seed, for at least 40 items overall.
Include at least 3 engagements executed with co-source specialists so the co-source oversight is tested.
Record population size, seed and selection date for reproducibility.
testing.done: the sample covers all critical findings and CIF engagements plus a reproducible random selection including co-sourced work.

testing.step: Re-perform the auditor ICT competence assessment
actions: Take the auditors who actually charged time to each sampled engagement and pull their certifications and role history from the HRIS independently of the audit file.
Test against the Art. 6(6) expectation of sufficient ICT knowledge, skills and expertise for the domain audited, not for auditing generally.
Check the independence record - any auditor who previously designed or operated the audited control is an exception.
Where competence rested on a co-source firm, confirm the engagement contract scope covers the domain and the specialist actually charged time.
testing.done: every sampled engagement has independently verified auditor competence for its domain and a clean independence record.

testing.step: Re-perform selected audit testing to challenge the conclusion
actions: For 5 sampled engagements pick the key control the opinion most depends on and re-read the workpaper's test method, sample and evidence.
Confirm the test went beyond inquiry - inspection or re-performance evidence must be present for a key ICT control.
Redraw a small sub-sample from the same population and re-perform the test to see whether the recorded conclusion holds.
Log any engagement where the conclusion is not supported by the evidence on file as an exception.
testing.done: the key control behind each of 5 sampled opinions is re-performed and any unsupported conclusion is logged.

testing.step: Test closure evidence on every critical finding
actions: For each critical finding closed in the year open the closure record and look for a post-remediation re-performance workpaper.
Confirm the re-test sample was drawn after the remediation date - a re-test on pre-remediation data is a failed closure.
Check the re-test addressed the recorded cause and not only the sampled symptom.
Treat any closure supported only by a management assertion or a screenshot supplied by the owner as an exception.
testing.done: every critical closure is supported by post-remediation re-performance evidence or logged as a closure exception.

testing.step: Recompute finding ageing and the follow-up SLA
actions: Recompute days between raise date and agreed date, and between agreed date and actual closure, for every sampled finding.
Flag every critical finding closed more than 90 days after its agreed date and every date extension granted without committee visibility.
Check the audit trail for agreed dates edited after the report was issued.
Compare the recomputed open-critical ageing to the figures reported to the audit committee each quarter.
testing.done: finding ageing is recomputed from raw dates and every difference from the reported committee figures is explained.

testing.step: Trace reporting and escalation to primary committee records
actions: Open the audit committee papers and minutes for each quarter and confirm the follow-up register was tabled with open critical findings by age band.
Confirm every critical finding past 30 days appears in the minutes with either a new date or a CRO-signed risk acceptance.
Trace each recorded risk acceptance to an entry in the ICT risk register in the GRC platform.
Capture the minute extracts into the workpaper.
testing.done: quarterly follow-up reporting is evidenced in the minutes and every overdue critical finding has a minuted outcome traced to the risk register.

testing.step: Log exceptions with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise one issue per exception naming the Art. 6(6) or 6(7) element missed and its supervisory consequence.

Assign a root cause from the list - plan not approved in time, engagement deferred without approval, competence not evidenced, testing relied on inquiry, closure without re-performance, follow-up reporting incomplete.
Name an owner and a remediation date, routing any exception concerning the Chief Audit Executive's own function to the audit committee chair.
Carry every open exception into next year's quality review as a mandatory retest row.
testing.done: every exception has an issue, a coded root cause, an owner, a remediation date and a retest commitment.

testing.step: Conclude, obtain independent sign-off and report
actions: Summarise plan completion percentage, engagements without evidenced competence, critical closures without re-performance and critical findings past 90 days.
State a conclusion - effective, effective with exceptions, or ineffective - against the thresholds set for this obligation.
Have the reviewer, who sits outside internal audit and performed none of the audits, sign the workpaper with name and date.
Report the conclusion directly to the audit committee chair and file the signed workpaper under DORA/Art-6-6 in the compliance evidence repository.
testing.done: a signed workpaper carries the coverage, competence and closure statistics, a stated conclusion and a recorded report to the committee chair.

Compliance procedure approved.value: Approved by the Chief Info Security Officer under the management-body-approved information security policy; reviewed at least yearly and out of cycle whenever an algorithm is deprecated, a major incident exposes a control gap, or Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1774 is amended

checklist.step: Define the control scope from the CIF asset inventory
actions: Export from the CMDB every ICT asset supporting a critical or important function, with asset class, environment, data classification, hosting model and system owner.
Tag each asset with the Art. 9 controls that must apply - MFA, PAM brokering, encryption at rest, encryption in transit, configuration baseline, network segment.
Reconcile the CMDB asset list against the IAM platform's application catalogue and the cloud subscription inventory and chase every asset present in one and absent from another.
Publish the scoped inventory to the Chief Info Security Officer and freeze it as the quarter's control population.
checklist.done: a reconciled CIF asset inventory exists with the required Art. 9 controls tagged per asset and frozen as the quarter's population.

checklist.step: Enforce multi-factor authentication across the in-scope estate
actions: In the IAM platform open Security ▸ Authentication Policies and set a policy requiring phishing-resistant MFA for all remote access, all administrative access and all access to CIF applications.
Run the MFA enrolment report and list every account in scope that is unenrolled, using a service-account or legacy-protocol reason where it applies.
Disable legacy authentication protocols that bypass MFA and confirm from the sign-in logs that no successful legacy authentication remains.
Route each residual unenrolled account to the CISO as a time-bound exception with a compensating control, or block it.
Publish weekly MFA coverage by application to the IT Security Manager.
checklist.done: MFA policy covers every remote, administrative and CIF application access path, with legacy authentication proven closed and residual accounts under dated exceptions.

checklist.step: Broker all privileged access through the PAM platform
actions: Onboard every privileged account on a CIF system into CyberArk so credentials are vaulted, rotated after use and never known to the user.
Convert standing administrative entitlements to just-in-time elevation with a ticket reference and an approver, and set a maximum session duration.
Enable session recording and keystroke logging for privileged sessions on CIF systems and confirm recordings are retained per the standard.
Define the break-glass procedure - sealed credentials, dual authorisation, automatic alert to the SOC Lead on use, and a mandatory post-use review within 1 business day.
Report any privileged account still authenticating outside the vault to the Chief Info Security Officer weekly.
checklist.done: privileged access to CIF systems runs through the vault with just-in-time elevation and session recording, and out-of-vault use is reported weekly.

checklist.step: Run the joiner process so access is granted from an approved role model
actions: Take the joiner event from the HRIS feed and provision only the birthright entitlements defined for the person's role in the role model.
Route any entitlement beyond birthright to the application owner for approval before provisioning, and record the approval reference on the request.
Refuse requests that name no business justification or that copy another user's access wholesale, which is how entitlement creep starts.
Confirm the account was created with MFA enrolment enforced at first sign-in.
checklist.done: each joiner receives only role-model birthright access plus individually approved additions, with MFA enforced at first sign-in.

checklist.step: Run the mover process so old access is removed, not just added to
actions: Trigger a mover review on every HRIS job or department change and present the leaving role's entitlements for explicit removal.
Require the new line manager to approve retained entitlements individually rather than accepting the existing set by default.
Complete removal within 5 business days of the effective transfer date and record the completion timestamp.
Report movers with retained entitlements from two or more roles to the IT Security Manager as segregation-of-duties risk.
checklist.done: every mover has the prior role's entitlements explicitly removed or individually re-approved within 5 business days.

checklist.step: Revoke leaver access inside the 24-hour clock
actions: Consume the HRIS termination record and disable the primary identity immediately, which cascades to federated applications.
Revoke non-federated and local application accounts, VPN certificates, privileged vault access and API keys held by the leaver, working from the entitlement report rather than memory.
Terminate active sessions and rotate any shared credential the leaver knew.
Record the termination timestamp and the revocation timestamp on the case so the elapsed time is measurable.
Page the on-call access team where a revocation is still open at 24 hours.
checklist.done: every leaver has all identities, credentials and API keys revoked with recorded timestamps inside 24 hours of the HR termination record.

checklist.step: Run the quarterly access recertification campaign
actions: Launch a certification campaign 15 days before quarter end covering all entitlements on CIF systems and all privileged entitlements everywhere.
Route each entitlement to the application owner or line manager with the entitlement's plain-language description, not its technical group name.
Set revocation to execute automatically on any entitlement not certified by the campaign close date rather than defaulting to retain.
Chase reviewers at day 7 and day 12 and escalate non-responders to their executive at day 14.
Publish completion percentage, revocation count and non-responder list to the Chief Info Security Officer at campaign close.
checklist.done: the campaign closes at 100 percent of in-scope entitlements reviewed, with uncertified entitlements auto-revoked and results published.

checklist.step: Hunt down orphaned, shared and service accounts
actions: Join the identity store to the HRIS active-worker list and list accounts with no matching worker as orphans.
List accounts with interactive logon and no unique human owner as shared accounts and assign each a named accountable owner or close it.
Inventory service and machine accounts on CIF systems with their purpose, owner, credential rotation interval and last use date.
Disable accounts unused for 90 days after notifying the owner, and delete after a further 90 days.
Report the orphan and shared-account counts monthly with the movement since last month.
checklist.done: orphan and shared accounts on CIF systems are closed or assigned a named owner, and dormant accounts are disabled on the 90-day rule.

checklist.step: Encrypt CIF data at rest and in transit to the cryptographic standard
actions: Build an encryption inventory of every CIF data store - databases, object storage, backups, endpoints - recording the algorithm, key length and key custodian.
Enforce transport encryption at TLS 1.2 or above with approved cipher suites on every CIF endpoint and disable deprecated protocol versions at the load balancer.
Scan externally facing CIF endpoints to confirm the negotiated protocol and cipher match the standard rather than trusting the configuration file.
Escalate any CIF data store that cannot be encrypted to the Chief Info Security Officer for a dated exception with compensating controls.
File the inventory and the scan output as the quarter's encryption evidence.
checklist.done: every CIF data store and endpoint is recorded in the encryption inventory with an approved algorithm, proven by scan output or covered by a dated exception.

checklist.step: Manage the cryptographic key and certificate lifecycle
actions: Maintain the key and certificate register with issuer, subject, key length, custodian, issue date, expiry date and rotation interval.
Set automated alerts at 90, 30 and 7 days before expiry that open an ITSM task assigned to the custodian.
Rotate keys at the interval the cryptographic standard sets and after any suspected compromise, recording the rotation with dual control.
Store private keys in the hardware security module or the platform key vault, never in source code or configuration files, and run a secret-scanning job over the code repository to prove it.
checklist.done: every key and certificate has a register entry, armed expiry alerts and a recorded rotation, with secret scanning proving no private key sits in code.

checklist.step: Hold network segmentation and configuration baselines
actions: Document the network zones and the permitted flows between them, with CIF systems isolated from general corporate and internet-facing zones.
Apply hardened configuration baselines to CIF hosts and network devices and scan for drift at least weekly.
Route every firewall rule change through the Change Coordinator with a business justification, an owner and a review date, and review rules with no traffic hits every 6 months.
Report segmentation violations and baseline drift to the IT Security Manager weekly with remediation owners.
checklist.done: CIF systems sit in documented isolated zones with weekly baseline drift scanning and reviewed, justified firewall rules.

checklist.step: Monitor the controls continuously in the SIEM
actions: Ingest authentication, privileged session, entitlement change, configuration change and key management events from the IAM platform, CyberArk, the cloud control plane and CIF applications.
Build detections for MFA bypass, privileged access outside the vault, entitlement granted without an approval record, disabled logging and mass entitlement change.
Set alert thresholds and route each detection to the SOC queue with a named response playbook.
Confirm daily that every in-scope source is still reporting, and treat a silent log source as an incident rather than a data-quality issue.
checklist.done: all in-scope control telemetry lands in the SIEM with detections routed to playbooks and silent log sources handled as incidents.

checklist.step: Govern control exceptions with owners and expiry dates
actions: Record every exception - MFA, standing privilege, unencrypted store, unsupported protocol - with the affected asset, the reason, the compensating control, the owner and an expiry date.
Refuse any exception request that names no compensating control or no expiry date.
Review the exception register monthly with the IT Security Manager and close or renew each item on its expiry - renewal requires fresh CISO approval.
Report exception count and age to the Chief Info Security Officer monthly and to the risk committee quarterly.
checklist.done: every control exception carries a compensating control, an owner and an expiry date, and is renewed only with fresh CISO approval.

checklist.step: Report control health and drive remediation
actions: Publish the monthly control dashboard - MFA coverage, PAM brokering coverage, JML SLA attainment, recertification completeness, encryption coverage, open exceptions - by CIF system.
Set a remediation owner and date for every metric below target and review progress fortnightly with the Head of IT.
Escalate any CIF system below target for two consecutive months to the risk committee.
Feed the metric trend into the annual Art. 24 testing scope so weak controls get tested harder.
checklist.done: the monthly dashboard reports control coverage per CIF system and every below-target metric has an owner, a date and fortnightly review.

checklist.step: Retain the control evidence for supervisory production
actions: Each quarter file the pack - CIF asset inventory, MFA and PAM coverage reports, JML timing extract, recertification campaign results with reviewer decisions, encryption inventory and scan output, key rotation log, exception register.
File under DORA/Art-9/<year>-Q<n> with the 5-year retention label.
Index by CIF system, control type and quarter so a supervisor's question on one control can be answered without a rebuild.
Record the pack location on the DORA obligation record for the 10 business day production service level.
checklist.done: the quarterly control evidence pack is filed, retention-labelled and indexed by CIF system and control type.

testing.step: Build the identity, entitlement and asset population
actions: Extract all active identities and their entitlements on CIF-supporting systems as at the test date, with account type and last logon.
Extract all joiner, mover and leaver events in the quarter from the HRIS with effective dates.
Extract the CIF asset inventory from the CMDB and the encryption inventory from the security team.
Reconcile identity counts to the HRIS active-worker list and sign the population with extract timestamps.
testing.done: identity, JML, asset and encryption populations are extracted, reconciled to HRIS and signed with dated timestamps.

testing.step: Recompute leaver revocation timing against the 24-hour SLA
actions: For every leaver in the quarter compute elapsed hours between the HRIS termination effective time and the last entitlement revocation timestamp.
Flag every case above 24 hours and every case where an entitlement is still active at the test date.
Check federated and non-federated systems separately - the primary identity being disabled does not prove a local application account was closed.
Compute the SLA attainment rate independently and compare it to the figure on the monthly dashboard.
testing.done: revocation timing is recomputed for every leaver and every breach of the 24-hour SLA is listed with its still-active entitlements.

testing.step: Draw a documented sample of identities, sessions and assets
actions: Take 100 percent of privileged accounts on CIF systems and 100 percent of leavers with any revocation past 24 hours.
Take 25 standard identities at random on CIF systems using a recorded seed, plus 10 privileged sessions and 10 CIF data stores.
Include at least 5 joiners and 5 movers so the whole lifecycle is covered.
Record population size, seed and selection date so the sample can be redrawn.
testing.done: the sample covers all CIF privileged accounts plus a reproducible selection across joiners, movers, sessions and data stores.

testing.step: Re-perform MFA and PAM coverage from source telemetry
actions: Query the SIEM for successful authentications to CIF applications in the quarter and identify any authenticated without a second factor.
Query privileged logons on CIF systems and identify any that did not originate from a CyberArk brokered session.
Compare the results to the MFA and PAM coverage figures reported on the dashboard and explain any difference.
For each gap check whether a dated CISO exception exists, treating an undocumented gap as a fail.
testing.done: MFA and PAM coverage are recomputed from authentication telemetry and every gap is matched to a dated exception or logged as a fail.

testing.step: Re-perform the entitlement judgement on sampled identities
actions: For each sampled identity list current entitlements and compare them to the role model birthright set for the person's HRIS role.
For every entitlement beyond birthright trace to an individual approval record naming the approver and the date.
Test for segregation-of-duties conflicts using the conflict matrix - for example the ability both to create and to approve a payment or a change.
Log entitlements with no approval, an approver who is the requester, or an unresolved conflict as exceptions.
testing.done: every sampled entitlement traces to birthright or an independent approval, and conflicts are tested against the matrix.

testing.step: Test recertification completeness and reviewer diligence
actions: Take the quarter's campaign and recompute the percentage of in-scope entitlements actually decided, not the percentage of reviewers who responded.
Confirm entitlements left undecided at close were auto-revoked and trace 10 of them to the revocation record.
Look for rubber-stamping - reviewers approving every entitlement within a few minutes across large populations - and sample 5 such decisions for supporting justification.
Confirm the campaign scope actually included every CIF system in the frozen inventory.
testing.done: recertification completeness is recomputed, auto-revocations are traced, and rubber-stamped decisions are sampled for justification.

testing.step: Verify encryption configuration on sampled data stores and endpoints
actions: For each sampled CIF data store read the live encryption configuration from the platform rather than the inventory record and note algorithm and key length.
Scan the sampled external endpoints and record the negotiated TLS version and cipher suite, flagging any deprecated protocol still accepted.
Confirm the key protecting each sampled store sits in the HSM or platform key vault and has been rotated inside its stated interval.
Log any difference between the live configuration and the encryption inventory as a data-integrity exception in its own right.
testing.done: encryption is verified live for every sampled store and endpoint, with inventory mismatches logged separately from control failures.

testing.step: Test break-glass and privileged session evidence
actions: List every break-glass credential use in the quarter and confirm each triggered an alert to the SOC Lead and a post-use review inside 1 business day.
Open 10 sampled privileged session recordings and confirm they exist, are complete and are attributable to a named human.
Trace each sampled session to a ticket reference and an approver, and confirm the elevation ended within the maximum session duration.
Confirm credentials were rotated after use as the vault policy requires.
testing.done: every break-glass use has an alert and a timely post-use review, and sampled sessions are attributable, ticketed and time-bound.

testing.step: Log exceptions with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise one issue per exception naming the Art. 9 or Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1774 requirement missed and the CIF systems affected.
Assign a root cause from the list - HR feed delay, non-federated account missed, role model stale, approval bypassed, reviewer rubber-stamped, encryption not applied at build, key not rotated.
Name an owner in the accountable IT team and set a remediation date inside 30 days for anything touching a CIF system.
Carry every open exception into the next quarter's test as a mandatory retest row.
testing.done: every exception has an issue, a coded root cause, an owner, a remediation date inside 30 days for CIF systems, and a retest commitment.

testing.step: Conclude, obtain independent sign-off and report
actions: Compute the quarter's statistics - leaver SLA attainment, MFA and PAM coverage, recertification completeness, encryption coverage, open exceptions past expiry.
State a conclusion - effective, effective with exceptions, or ineffective - against the zero-tolerance thresholds for leaver revocation and CIF privileged access.
Have the reviewer, who holds no administrative entitlement on the tested systems and performed no provisioning in the period, sign the workpaper with name and date.
Report to the risk committee and file the signed workpaper under DORA/Art-9 in the compliance evidence repository.
testing.done: a signed workpaper carries the quarter's control statistics, a stated conclusion and a recorded risk committee reporting date.

Accountable obligation owner.value: Owns the Art. 10 anomalous-activity detection layers, the Art. 17 ICT-related incident management process and the annual incident response plan exercise; the Chief Info Security Officer owns the decision to classify an incident as major and the submission to the competent authority

Citation verified against current regula.value: Yes - Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 Art. 10(1)-(3) on detection and Art. 17(1)-(3) on the incident management process, read with Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1774 Art. 12 on logging and with the major-incident classification and reporting RTS/ITS, all checked on EUR-Lex at the annual plan review

In-scope processes.value: Log collection and detection engineering -> alert triage and single-point-of-failure identification -> ICT incident recording, classification and severity assignment -> major-incident determination against the Art. 18 criteria -> initial, intermediate and final regulatory notification -> client communication where clients are affected -> root cause analysis and post-incident review -> annual incident response plan exercise

In-scope systems.value: The SIEM/SOAR ingests the Art. 12 log sources and runs the detection rules and playbooks; CrowdStrike Falcon supplies endpoint detection; the ITSM/security ticketing system is the incident record of truth including classification fields and notification timestamps

Compliance procedure documented.value: ICT Incident Management Procedure - log source catalogue and retention, alert thresholds and triage SLAs, the ICT incident severity scale, the Art. 18 major-incident classification decision tree with its quantitative thresholds, the notification runbook with the 4/24/72-hour and one-month clocks, client notification criteria and templates, and the annual exercise standard

Compliance procedure approved.value: Approved by the Chief Info Security Officer and noted by the management body; reviewed at least yearly, after every major incident, and whenever the ESAs update the classification thresholds or the reporting templates

Filing/reporting deadlines tracked.value: Initial notification to the competent authority within 4 hours of classifying an incident as major and in any case no later than 24 hours from becoming aware of it; intermediate report within 72 hours of the initial notification and on every material status change; final report no later than one month after the intermediate report; clients informed without undue delay where their financial interests are affected; the incident response plan exercised at least annually

Deadline reminders configured.value: When an incident is flagged major in the ITSM system, timers start automatically and page the Incident Response Lead at 2 hours and the Chief Info Security Officer at 3 hours against the 4-hour initial clock, then at 48 hours against the 72-hour intermediate clock and at 3 weeks against the one-month final clock; the annual exercise sits on the resilience calendar with T-60 and T-30 reminders

Evidence retained per the retention requ.value: Incident records with full timeline, detection alerts, classification worksheets, submitted notification forms and their acknowledgements, client communications, root cause analyses and exercise reports retained 5 years and producible to the competent authority on request

Violations/exceptions logged with dispos.value: A missed 4-hour, 24-hour, 72-hour or one-month deadline, an incident classified major late, a detection gap that let an incident be found by a third party, and a client notification not sent where the criteria were met are each logged as a reportable compliance exception with root cause and owner

Remediation sign-off captured.value: The CISO signs the major-incident classification decision, every regulatory submission before it is sent, and the closure of each post-incident action arising from the root cause analysis

Test population (in-scope transactions,.value: All ICT-related incidents recorded in the period regardless of severity, all significant cyber threats notified voluntarily, the detection rule inventory against the log source catalogue, and the annual incident response plan exercise record

Pass/fail thresholds.value: Fail on any major incident whose initial notification exceeded 4 hours from classification or 24 hours from awareness, any intermediate report beyond 72 hours or final report beyond one month, any incident that met the Art. 18 major criteria but was not classified major, any client-affecting incident with no client communication, or a year with no incident response plan exercise; each is reported individually to the risk committee

Compliance test frequency matched to the.value: The obligation is event-driven for notification and annual for the exercise, so testing is monthly over that month's incidents for classification and timeliness, plus an annual review of the exercise, detection coverage and the plan itself

Independent reviewer (segregated from th.value: The auditor must not have handled, classified or reported any sampled incident and must be able to pull the SIEM and ITSM extracts directly

Evidence location for test results.value: Monthly incident compliance workpaper and the annual detection and exercise review - incident population, classification re-performance, notification clock recomputation, detection coverage analysis and exception log - in the compliance evidence repository under DORA/Art-17

Regulator-ready documentation.value: Incident register export, per-incident classification worksheets, submitted initial, intermediate and final reports with acknowledgements, client communications, root cause analyses and the annual exercise report, producible to the competent authority within 5 business days

Regulator response path.value: The Chief Info Security Officer submits and owns dialogue with the competent authority on incidents; the Head of Compliance coordinates and logs every exchange; Legal Counsel clears any submission that concedes a missed deadline or a client detriment

checklist.step: Maintain the log source catalogue the detection layer depends on
actions: List every CIF-supporting system from the CMDB and record which logs it must emit - authentication, privileged action, configuration change, network flow, application error, data access.
Compare that list to the sources actually reporting into the SIEM and raise an onboarding task for every gap, naming the system owner.
Set retention on each source to the period the ICT Incident Management Procedure requires and confirm the index actually holds it.
Run a daily heartbeat check and treat any source silent for more than 4 hours as an incident, not a housekeeping item.
Report source coverage by CIF system to the SOC Lead weekly.
checklist.done: every CIF system's required log sources are onboarded with retention set, and silent sources raise an incident within 4 hours.

checklist.step: Engineer the detection rules and set alert thresholds
actions: Build detections across the layers Art. 10 requires - network performance degradation, unusual authentication, privilege escalation, data exfiltration volume, batch and interface failure, third-party connection anomalies.
Set an explicit numeric threshold and time window on each rule and record the rationale, since Art. 10(3) expects defined alert thresholds and criteria that trigger the incident response process.
Attach a named response playbook to every rule so an alert has a route rather than a queue.
Tune false positives weekly with the SOC Analyst team and record each tuning change with its author and date so sensitivity reductions are visible.
Map the rule set to the CIF list and report any CIF system with no detection coverage to the Chief Info Security Officer.
checklist.done: every detection rule has a numeric threshold, a rationale and a playbook, and no CIF system sits without detection coverage.

checklist.step: Identify single points of failure and wire them into monitoring
actions: Walk each CIF dependency chain in the CMDB and mark components with no redundancy, no failover or a single provider as single points of failure.
Confirm each identified single point of failure carries availability monitoring and an alert threshold in the SIEM.
Feed the list to the Business Continuity Manager so the next scenario test targets them.
Review the list quarterly and after every architecture change to a CIF chain.
checklist.done: every CIF single point of failure is identified, monitored with an alert threshold and handed to continuity testing.

checklist.step: Triage alerts into ICT incident records within the SLA
actions: Work the SOC queue in priority order and record the alert acknowledgement time against the triage SLA of 15 minutes for high-severity alerts.
Open an ICT incident record for every alert that is not disproved, capturing detection time, detection source and the systems and functions affected.
Set the awareness timestamp deliberately - it is the moment the entity became aware of the incident and it starts the 24-hour regulatory clock.
Notify the Incident Response Lead immediately where a CIF is affected, and do not wait for confirmation of impact.
Record every disproved alert with the reason so a wrong dismissal can be found later.
checklist.done: each alert is acknowledged inside SLA and either disproved with a recorded reason or converted into an incident with an explicit awareness timestamp.

checklist.step: Classify the incident against the Art. 18 major criteria
actions: Complete the classification worksheet as soon as impact is measurable - clients and financial counterparts affected and their number, transactions affected, reputational impact, duration and service downtime, geographical spread, data losses touching availability authenticity integrity or confidentiality, criticality of services affected and economic impact.
Apply the quantitative thresholds in the classification RTS to each criterion and record the measured value, not a judgement word.
Reach the major or not-major conclusion, record who decided and when, and route the decision to the Chief Info Security Officer for sign-off.
Re-run the classification whenever new impact data arrives - an incident can become major hours after it opened, and the clock runs from that classification.
Assess in parallel whether the event is a significant cyber threat that the entity will notify voluntarily.
checklist.done: a dated classification worksheet records a measured value against every Art. 18 criterion and a CISO-signed major or not-major decision.

checklist.step: File the initial notification inside the 4-hour and 24-hour clocks
actions: Start the clock from the classification decision time and confirm the earlier binding limit - 4 hours from classification as major, and never more than 24 hours from the awareness timestamp.

Complete the initial notification fields the reporting ITS requires - entity identifiers including LEI, incident reference, discovery and classification times, incident type, systems and functions affected, whether a major incident is confirmed or suspected, and whether other entities may be affected.
Have Legal Counsel review anything that states a cause or an attribution before submission, then submit through the competent authority's reporting channel.
Save the submission receipt with its timestamp onto the incident record and record the elapsed time against both clocks.
Where the 4-hour clock cannot be met, submit immediately and record the delay and its reason as a compliance exception rather than delaying further.
checklist.done: the initial notification is submitted inside 4 hours of classification and 24 hours of awareness, with the receipt and both elapsed times on the record.

checklist.step: Inform affected clients without undue delay
actions: Test the incident against the client-communication criteria - where a major ICT-related incident has or may have an impact on the financial interests of clients, they must be informed without undue delay.
Build the affected-client population from the incident scope with the Data Protection Officer, and reconcile it to the policy or account records rather than estimating.

Draft the notice stating what happened, what data or service was affected, the measures taken to mitigate the adverse effects, and what the client should do, and have Legal Counsel and the Privacy Officer clear it.
Issue through the channels the clients are reachable on - portal notice, email, letter for the unreachable - and record the send date and the recipient count.
Track inbound complaints arising from the notice through the Complaints Manager and report volumes daily while the incident is open.
checklist.done: affected clients are identified from records, notified with the mitigation measures stated, and the send date, recipient count and complaint volumes are recorded.

checklist.step: File the intermediate report inside 72 hours and on material change
actions: Assemble the updated position - current impact figures, systems restored, transactions affected, temporary measures applied and whether regular activities have resumed.

Submit the intermediate report within 72 hours of the initial notification, and resubmit whenever there is a material change in status or the handling of the incident changes based on new information.
Correct any figure that has moved since the initial notification explicitly rather than silently restating it.
Store the receipt and update the incident timeline with each submission.
checklist.done: the intermediate report is submitted inside 72 hours with corrected figures explicitly flagged, and every material change triggers a resubmission.

checklist.step: Run root cause analysis and file the final report inside one month
actions: Preserve forensic evidence at the outset - memory captures, disk images, log exports with hashes - so the analysis is defensible.
Establish the root cause and the contributing factors, distinguishing the technical trigger from the control failure that let it matter.
Quantify the direct and indirect costs and losses and the recoveries, since these feed the aggregated annual figure the authority may request.
Complete the final report with root cause, remediation applied and permanent measures, and submit no later than one month after the intermediate report.
Where the root cause is not yet established at the deadline, submit on time with the position reached and the date the analysis will conclude.
checklist.done: the final report is submitted inside one month of the intermediate report with a stated root cause, quantified costs and permanent measures.

checklist.step: Convert post-incident findings into tracked actions
actions: Hold the post-incident review within 10 business days of resolution with the responders, the system owner and the Chief Info Security Officer.
Raise a GRC action for every control failure identified, with an owner at director level and a date, and link it to the incident record.
Update the ICT risk register where the incident showed a risk was mis-scored or a control was ineffective.
Feed detection gaps back to the Threat Detection Engineer as new rules and the response gaps into the next exercise scenario.
Report action ageing to the risk committee until closure.
checklist.done: every post-incident control failure is a dated GRC action linked to the incident, with detection and response gaps fed into rules and exercises.

checklist.step: Exercise the incident response plan at least annually
actions: Pick a scenario the plan has not been tested against recently - ransomware on a CIF data store, a major provider outage, or an incident discovered by a client rather than by monitoring.
Run the exercise end to end including the regulatory notification steps, drafting a real initial notification against the 4-hour clock without submitting it.

Involve the Chief Info Security Officer, Legal Counsel, Communications Specialist, the Consumer Affairs Manager and the affected business owner so the decision chain is exercised, not just the technical response.
Time each phase - detection, triage, classification, notification draft, client communication draft, containment - and compare against the plan's stated targets.
Write the exercise report with gaps, owners and dates within 10 business days and update the plan accordingly.
checklist.done: an annual end-to-end exercise including the notification chain is run, timed against plan targets, and its gaps are owned and dated.

checklist.step: Keep the classification decision tree current with ESA guidance
actions: Monitor ESA publications, Q&As and reporting template updates for changes to the major-incident criteria, thresholds or fields.
Where a threshold moves, update the classification worksheet and the ITSM classification fields in the same change and record the effective date.
Brief the Incident Response Lead and the SOC Lead on the change and confirm the on-call responders know the current thresholds.
Test the updated worksheet against two closed historical incidents to confirm it still produces the right answer.
checklist.done: the classification worksheet and ITSM fields match the current ESA thresholds, with the change briefed and back-tested on historical incidents.

checklist.step: Report incident performance to the risk committee monthly
actions: Publish incident volume by severity, mean detection and containment times, major incidents and their notification timeliness against each clock, and open post-incident actions.
Show incidents detected by a third party or a client separately - they measure the detection layer's failure.
Name every missed regulatory deadline individually with its cause rather than reporting a percentage.
Take the committee's directions into the detection roadmap and the exercise plan.
checklist.done: the monthly report shows notification timeliness against every clock and names each missed deadline with its cause.

checklist.step: Maintain the incident evidence trail for supervisory review
actions: For each major incident assemble the pack - detection alert, incident record with full timeline, classification worksheet, all three submissions with receipts, client communications, root cause analysis and post-incident actions.
File under DORA/Art-17/<year>/<incident reference> with the 5-year retention label.
Index by incident reference, date, affected function and major or not-major so a supervisor's query on a single event is answerable directly.
Record the pack location on the DORA obligation record for the 5 business day production service level.
checklist.done: each major incident has a single indexed evidence pack holding detection through final report, retention-labelled and retrievable by reference.

checklist.step: Prove the notification clocks are armed in the tooling
actions: Configure the incident form so setting classification to Major starts the 4-hour, 24-hour, 72-hour and one-month timers from the correct base timestamps.
Set escalation paging at 2 and 3 hours against the 4-hour clock and at 48 hours against the 72-hour clock, routed to the Incident Response Lead and the Chief Info Security Officer.
Make the awareness timestamp, the classification timestamp and each submission timestamp mandatory fields that cannot be edited without an audit entry.
Test the configuration quarterly with a dummy incident and confirm the pages actually arrive.
checklist.done: the ITSM incident form starts every regulatory clock automatically from immutable timestamps, with paging proven by a quarterly dummy incident.

testing.step: Build the incident population independently of the incident team
actions: Export every ICT-related incident record in the period with awareness time, classification, severity, affected functions and closure date.
Pull the SIEM high-severity alert history for the same period and identify alerts closed without an incident record.
Add service desk major incidents and change-failure records so operational events that were never routed to security are visible.
Reconcile the three sources, investigate every alert with no incident, and sign the population as complete with extract timestamps.
testing.done: the incident population reconciles ITSM, SIEM alerts and service desk records, with every high-severity alert lacking an incident investigated.

testing.step: Draw a documented sample across severities
actions: Take 100 percent of incidents classified major and 100 percent of incidents affecting a critical or important function.
Take 25 further incidents at random from the remainder using a recorded seed, weighting toward those closed quickly at low severity where under-classification hides.
Include every incident detected by a client, a provider or a regulator rather than by internal monitoring.
Record population size, seed and selection date for reproducibility.
testing.done: the sample covers all major and CIF-affecting incidents plus a reproducible random selection weighted to fast low-severity closures.

testing.step: Re-perform the major-incident classification on the sample
actions: For each sampled incident gather the impact facts from the incident timeline and the affected system owners before reading the recorded classification.

Apply the Art. 18 criteria and the current quantitative thresholds independently - clients affected, transactions affected, downtime, geographical spread, data losses, criticality of services, economic impact.
Compare to the recorded decision and treat any incident that met a threshold but was not classified major as a reportable exception.
Check the classification date - a late classification shortens nothing, it simply moves the 4-hour clock, so test the 24-hour awareness limit separately.
Attach the independent worksheet to the workpaper.
testing.done: every sampled incident has an independent classification conclusion and each under-classification is logged as reportable.

testing.step: Recompute every notification clock from immutable timestamps
actions: For each major incident take the awareness timestamp, classification timestamp and submission timestamps from the ITSM audit history rather than the summary fields.
Compute hours from classification to initial submission against the 4-hour limit and hours from awareness to initial submission against the 24-hour limit.
Compute hours from initial to intermediate against 72 hours and days from intermediate to final against one month.
Check the audit history for edits to any timestamp after submission and treat an edited awareness time as an exception in its own right.
Trace each submission to a stored receipt from the competent authority.
testing.done: all four clocks are recomputed from immutable audit history, each traced to a stored receipt, with any post-hoc timestamp edit logged.

testing.step: Test client notification where the criteria were met
actions: For each sampled incident assess independently whether client financial interests were or may have been affected.
Where they were, confirm a client communication exists, read what it said about the incident and the mitigation measures, and compute the delay from awareness to issue.
Reconcile the notified recipient count to the affected-client population built from policy and account records rather than the estimate on the incident record.
Log any client-affecting incident with no communication, or a communication silent on mitigation measures, as an exception.
testing.done: every client-affecting incident is matched to a dated communication covering mitigation measures, with recipient counts reconciled to account records.

testing.step: Test detection coverage against the log source catalogue
actions: Compare the CIF system list from the CMDB to the log sources actually reporting into the SIEM during the period and compute coverage.
Identify every source that went silent for more than 4 hours and check an incident was raised.
For 10 sampled detection rules confirm a numeric threshold and a rationale exist and that a playbook is attached.
Review the tuning change history for sensitivity reductions and confirm each was approved rather than applied by the analyst alone.
testing.done: detection coverage is recomputed per CIF system, silent sources are matched to incidents, and rule tuning changes are traced to approvals.

testing.step: Test incidents found by third parties as detection failures
actions: List every incident whose discovery source was a client, a provider, a regulator or a public disclosure.
For each, establish from the SIEM whether the telemetry to detect it existed and was simply not alerted on, or whether the telemetry was absent altogether.
Confirm a detection gap action was raised and delivered - a new rule, a new log source or a threshold change - and trace it to production.
Report the count and trend of externally discovered incidents as an Art. 10 effectiveness measure.
testing.done: every externally discovered incident is analysed for whether telemetry existed, with a delivered detection action traced to production.

testing.step: Test the annual exercise and the post-incident action closure
actions: Confirm an incident response plan exercise took place in the last 12 months and read the report for scenario, participants and timings.
Check the exercise actually ran the regulatory notification and client communication steps rather than stopping at technical containment.
Take the exercise gaps and the post-incident actions from sampled incidents and trace each to closure evidence in the GRC platform.
Log actions closed on assertion, and any exercise gap that reappeared as a real incident cause, as exceptions.
testing.done: the annual exercise is evidenced end to end including notification, and every exercise and post-incident action traces to closure evidence.

testing.step: Log exceptions with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise one issue per exception naming the incident reference, the clock or criterion missed and the supervisory consequence.

Assign a root cause from the list - detection gap, triage delay, awareness timestamp set late, classification thresholds misapplied, approval chain slow, template fields unavailable, client population not identifiable.
Name an owner and a remediation date, and where a regulatory deadline was missed require a self-report decision from the Chief Info Security Officer and Legal Counsel.
Carry every open exception into the next month's test as a mandatory retest row.
testing.done: every exception has an issue, a coded root cause, an owner, a remediation date and, for missed deadlines, a recorded self-report decision.

testing.step: Conclude, obtain independent sign-off and report
actions: Summarise major incidents in the period, timeliness against each of the four clocks, under-classifications found, externally discovered incidents and client notification performance.
State a conclusion - effective, effective with exceptions, or ineffective - against the zero-missed-deadline and zero-under-classification thresholds.
Have the reviewer, who handled, classified and reported none of the sampled incidents, sign the workpaper with name and date.
Report to the risk committee and the management body and file the signed workpaper under DORA/Art-17 in the compliance evidence repository.
testing.done: a signed workpaper carries per-clock timeliness statistics, a stated conclusion and a recorded committee reporting date.

Accountable obligation owner.value: Owns and certifies the annual Art. 11(10) estimation of aggregated annual costs and losses caused by major ICT-related incidents, and the accompanying Art. 6(5) certification that the ICT risk management framework was reviewed; the Operational Risk Manager assembles the loss data and the Controller validates the financial amounts

Citation verified against current regula.value: Yes - Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 Art. 11(10) on the aggregated cost and loss estimation provided to the competent authority on request, Art. 6(5) on documenting and reviewing the ICT risk management framework at least yearly and after major incidents, and Arts. 25(1)-(3) on testing ICT tools and systems, all read on EUR-Lex at each annual certification

In-scope processes.value: Major ICT incident register close -> per-incident cost and loss capture across direct costs, indirect losses and recoveries -> reconciliation to the general ledger and the operational risk loss database -> aggregation to the financial year figure -> Art. 6(5) framework review attestation -> executive certification and management body noting -> production to the competent authority on request

In-scope systems.value: The ERP general ledger holds the booked costs, provisions, redress and recoveries the estimate reconciles to; the GRC platform holds the operational risk loss events and the framework review record; the ITSM incident register supplies the major-incident population the estimate covers

Compliance procedure documented.value: Annual ICT Cost and Loss Certification Procedure - the cost taxonomy (response labour, forensics and external specialists, hardware and software replacement, communications and redress, legal and regulatory costs, lost revenue and business interruption), the recovery taxonomy (insurance settlements, provider service credits, third-party recoveries), the estimation method for costs that cannot be booked, the reconciliation rules, and the certification wording

Compliance procedure approved.value: Approved by the Chief Financial Officer and the Chief Info Security Officer jointly, because the figure has to satisfy both a supervisory definition and an accounting reconciliation; re-approved each year before the estimation cycle opens

Filing/reporting deadlines tracked.value: Annual cycle tied to the financial year - loss data cut at year end, estimation complete within 60 days of year end, certification signed within 90 days, and the pack held ready for production to the competent authority within 10 business days of any request under Art. 11(10); the Art. 6(5) framework review is completed at least yearly and re-opened after any major ICT-related incident

Deadline reminders configured.value: GRC calendar drives the cycle - T-30 days before year end a data-completeness notice to incident owners and Finance, day 15 reconciliation to the ledger, day 45 draft to the CFO and CISO, day 60 estimation locked, day 90 certification signed; a standing task holds the pack in a production-ready state between cycles

Evidence retained per the retention requ.value: Per-incident cost worksheets with source references, the ledger reconciliation, the loss database extract, the estimation method note, the signed certification and the management body minute retained 5 years from certification and produced with the estimate whenever the authority asks

Violations/exceptions logged with dispos.value: A major incident with no cost worksheet, an unreconciled difference to the general ledger above the materiality threshold, an estimate certified without Controller validation, and a late certification are each logged as an issue with an owner and a correction date

Remediation sign-off captured.value: The CFO validates that the aggregated figure reconciles to booked costs, provisions and recoveries in the general ledger and countersigns the certification alongside the Chief Info Security Officer

Test population (in-scope transactions,.value: Every incident classified major in the financial year, every general ledger posting to the ICT incident cost centres and the related provisions and recoveries, and every operational risk loss event tagged to an ICT cause in the loss database

Pass/fail thresholds.value: Fail if any major incident in the year has no cost worksheet, if the aggregated figure differs from the reconciled ledger and loss database position by more than the agreed materiality threshold without a documented explanation, if any estimated component lacks a stated method and basis, if the Controller did not validate the amounts, or if the certification was signed after day 90

Compliance test frequency matched to the.value: The obligation is an annual estimate produced on supervisory request, so assurance runs once a year over the certified figure, plus a half-year interim check that cost worksheets are being completed as incidents close rather than reconstructed in January

Independent reviewer (segregated from th.value: The auditor must not have prepared any cost worksheet, performed the reconciliation or drafted the certification, and must pull the ledger extract directly from Finance systems

Evidence location for test results.value: Annual ICT cost and loss certification workpaper - major incident population, worksheet coverage, ledger reconciliation re-performance, estimation method review and exception log - in the compliance evidence repository under DORA/Art-11-10/<financial year>

Regulator-ready documentation.value: The signed certification, the aggregated estimate with its breakdown by cost and recovery category, the per-incident schedule, the ledger reconciliation and the method note, packaged for the competent authority within 10 business days of an Art. 11(10) request

Regulator response path.value: The Chief Info Security Officer submits the estimate on request, the Chief Financial Officer answers questions on the financial derivation, and the Head of Compliance logs the request, the response and any follow-up; Legal Counsel clears any commentary on unresolved litigation or redress exposure

checklist.step: Open the annual cycle and freeze the major-incident population
actions: Export every incident classified major in the financial year with incident reference, classification date, affected functions, duration and closure date.
Add incidents classified major after year end whose impact fell inside the year, and flag them so the cut-off treatment is visible.
Cross-check against the regulatory submissions filed in the year - any incident notified to the authority as major must appear in the population.
Notify each incident owner 30 days before year end that a cost worksheet is due, listing their open incidents.
Lock the population with a timestamp and row count as the basis of the estimate.
checklist.done: the major-incident population is locked, timestamped and reconciled to the regulatory notifications filed during the year.

checklist.step: Capture direct response costs per incident
actions: For each incident collect internal response effort from the incident timeline and the time recording system, and price it at the standard internal cost rate agreed with Finance.

Pull external costs from the ledger - forensic firms, incident response retainers, specialist counsel, crisis communications - by matching purchase orders and invoices carrying the incident reference.
Add hardware and software replacement, emergency cloud capacity and overtime booked against the incident cost centre.
Where an invoice covers several incidents, apportion on a stated basis and record the basis on the worksheet.
Attach the ledger document numbers to each line so every amount is traceable.
checklist.done: each incident's direct costs are itemised, priced on agreed rates and traceable to ledger document numbers or timesheet records.

checklist.step: Capture indirect losses and client redress
actions: Quantify business interruption using the lost transaction or premium volume for the outage window, with the method agreed with the Chief Financial Officer.
Pull client redress, goodwill payments and complaint settlements arising from the incident from the complaints and payments records via the Complaints Manager.
Add regulatory penalties, litigation costs and provisions raised in respect of the incident, taking the provision balance and movement from the ledger.
Record contract penalties and service credits the entity paid to its own clients as losses, distinct from credits it received.
Mark every estimated amount as estimated with its method and the data behind it, rather than presenting it as booked.
checklist.done: indirect losses, redress, provisions and penalties are quantified per incident with estimated amounts explicitly flagged and methods stated.

checklist.step: Capture recoveries and net the figure correctly
actions: List insurance recoveries received and receivable against each incident, taking the claim reference and the settlement or reserve position from the insurance programme records.
List service credits and contractual recoveries from ICT third-party providers, sourced from the Vendor Manager and the contract terms.
Present gross costs, recoveries and net losses as separate columns - netting them into a single figure hides the exposure the supervisor is asking about.
Where a recovery is expected but unsettled, disclose it as receivable with its expected timing rather than including it in received recoveries.
checklist.done: gross costs, recoveries received and recoveries receivable are presented separately per incident, with unsettled amounts disclosed as such.

checklist.step: Reconcile the incident costs to the general ledger
actions: Extract postings to the ICT incident cost centres, the related provisions accounts and the recovery accounts for the financial year.
Match the ledger postings to the per-incident worksheets on document number and list both unmatched directions.
Explain each reconciling item - internal labour not booked to the ledger, apportioned invoices, provisions raised centrally, recoveries booked to another entity.
Set and document a materiality threshold with the Chief Financial Officer and require a written explanation for any unexplained difference above it.
Sign the reconciliation and attach it to the estimation pack.
checklist.done: the per-incident worksheets reconcile to ledger postings with every reconciling item explained and any residual above materiality explained in writing.

checklist.step: Reconcile to the operational risk loss database
actions: Extract operational risk loss events for the year tagged to an ICT or business disruption cause with gross loss, recovery and net loss amounts.
Match them to the major-incident population and investigate ICT loss events with no major incident and major incidents with no loss event.
Align the amounts or explain the definitional difference - the operational risk threshold and the DORA population are not the same and the difference must be stated, not smoothed.
Record the reconciliation as an appendix so the supervisor can see the two views agree.
checklist.done: the estimate reconciles to the operational risk loss database with every definitional difference stated rather than smoothed.

checklist.step: Document the estimation method for amounts that cannot be booked
actions: Write a method note covering each estimated component - internal labour rates, business interruption volume basis, apportionment rules, provision treatment and the treatment of costs spanning financial years.
State the data sources, the assumptions and the sensitivity of the aggregate to the two or three largest assumptions.
Have the Chief Financial Officer approve the method before the figure is locked, and keep the prior year's method alongside so changes are visible.
Where the method changed, restate the prior year on the new basis for comparability and label it as restated.
checklist.done: a CFO-approved method note covers every estimated component with assumptions, sensitivities and any prior-year restatement labelled.

checklist.step: Aggregate the annual figure and build the breakdown
actions: Aggregate gross costs, recoveries and net losses across the population and break them down by cost category, by affected critical or important function and by incident.
Show the largest incidents individually - a supervisor asking for the aggregate will ask next what drove it.
Compare against the prior two years and explain material movements in a short commentary.
Lock the workbook, version it, and record the extract dates behind each figure.
checklist.done: a locked, versioned aggregate with breakdowns by category, function and incident exists, with prior-year comparison and commentary.

checklist.step: Complete the Art. 6(5) framework review that accompanies the certification
actions: Review the ICT risk management framework document against the year's events - major incidents, Art. 24 test results, audit findings and third-party changes.
Record the review date, the reviewer, what changed and what was confirmed unchanged, since Art. 6(5) requires at least yearly review and review after major incidents.
Confirm each major incident in the year triggered its own framework review and that the outcome was recorded, not just the annual one.
Submit the revised framework to the management body for approval and record the approval date.
checklist.done: the framework review is recorded with date, reviewer and changes, and each major incident's own review outcome is evidenced.

checklist.step: Obtain the executive certification
actions: Prepare the certification wording naming the financial year, the aggregated gross cost, recoveries and net loss, the population covered and the method note version.
Include the statement that the ICT risk management framework was reviewed in accordance with Art. 6(5), with the review date.
Sign jointly with the Chief Financial Officer, who certifies the financial derivation, within 90 days of year end.
Disclose in the certification any known incomplete data - unsettled insurance claims, open litigation, provisions not yet quantified - rather than omitting it.
checklist.done: a jointly signed certification names the year, the aggregate figures, the population and the method version, with incomplete data disclosed.

checklist.step: Table the certification to the management body
